title: How I Built an AI-Powered Document Intelligence Platform Using Next.js, FastAPI, RAG and MCP
summary:
Introduction

In today's rapidly evolving world of Artificial Intelligence, I wanted to go beyond experimenting with Large Language Models (LLMs) and explore how AI can be integrated into real-world business workflows. My goal was to understand how AI systems can process unstructured data, extract meaningful information, validate results, and support decision-making while maintaining reliability and human oversight.

As organizations continue to handle growing volumes of invoices, reports, contracts, and other business documents, manual processing can become time-consuming and difficult to manage efficiently. I wanted to explore how modern AI technologies could help simplify these processes by combining intelligent document processing, automated workflows, and context-aware information retrieval into a single application.

That motivation led me to build the AI-Powered Document Intelligence & Approval Platform.

The idea was to create more than a traditional document management system. I wanted to explore how Large Language Models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and agentic workflows could work together to classify documents, extract structured information, apply validation rules, and make document content accessible through an AI-powered assistant. At the same time, I wanted to ensure that important business decisions remained under human control through a human-in-the-loop approval workflow.

To bring these ideas together, I worked with technologies including Next.js, TypeScript, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, LangChain, LangGraph, ChromaDB, OpenAI, Model Context Protocol (MCP), AWS S3, and Docker. Each technology helped me explore a different aspect of building a complete AI-powered application, from frontend development and backend API design to document retrieval, workflow orchestration, persistent storage, and external tool integration.

Throughout the development process, I explored how to connect AI capabilities with conventional software engineering practices such as authentication, role-based access control, document lifecycle management, and audit logging. This helped me better understand that building a useful AI application involves more than integrating an LLM; it requires designing a complete system around data quality, security, workflow reliability, and accountability.

In this article, I'll walk through the motivation behind the project, its architecture, the document processing pipeline, the RAG-powered assistant, the human approval workflow, the technologies I used, and the key lessons I learned while building the platform.

Project Repositories

  • Frontend: https://github.com/Madesh-cse/AI-Document-Approval-system-frontend
  • Backend: https://github.com/Madesh-cse/AI-Document-Approval-system-backend

From Documents to Decisions: Building an AI-Powered Document Intelligence & Approval Platform

Turning unstructured documents into actionable insights with LLMs, agentic workflows, RAG, and human-in-the-loop approval.

Every organization works with documents— invoices, contracts, reports, and business records. But behind every document lies a time-consuming process: extracting information, validating it, routing it to the right person, and tracking decisions.

Traditional document management systems help store and organize files, but they don't always understand their contents or automate the decisions that follow.

I wanted to explore how AI could bridge this gap, so I built an AI-Powered Document Intelligence & Approval Platform that combines document processing, intelligent retrieval, workflow automation, and human oversight in one system.

In this article, I'll walk through the architecture, key technologies, workflow design, and engineering decisions behind the project.

What Does the Platform Do?

The platform transforms uploaded documents into structured, searchable, and reviewable information.

Instead of manually reading every document and transferring its details into a system, users can upload a document and let the application handle the initial processing.

The platform supports:

  • Intelligent document processing: Classifies documents and extracts relevant information.
  • Validation guardrails: Checks extracted data before it proceeds through the workflow.
  • Human-in-the-loop approval: Allows managers to review, approve, or reject documents.
  • Document-specific AI assistant: Answers questions using the contents of a selected document.
  • Role-based access control: Separates permissions for administrators, managers, and employees.
  • Workflow automation: Uses MCP-based Google Calendar integration to schedule approval reviews.
  • Auditable document lifecycle: Tracks document status and approval activity.

The objective isn't to replace human decision-makers. It's to reduce repetitive work while keeping important decisions accountable.

Technology Stack

I selected the following technologies to build the application across the frontend, backend, AI, storage, and deployment layers.

Technology Purpose
Next.js, TypeScript Frontend and application interface
Tailwind CSS Responsive UI styling
Python, FastAPI Backend APIs and application logic
PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy Relational data persistence and ORM
LangChain LLM integration and retrieval components
LangGraph Stateful, multi-step AI workflows
OpenAI Language understanding, extraction, and question answering
ChromaDB Vector storage for document retrieval
AWS S3 Persistent document storage
MCP Integration with external tools, including Google Calendar
Docker Containerized application setup

Each component has a specific responsibility, helping keep the system modular and easier to maintain.

1. Designing the Document Processing Pipeline

A document upload is only the beginning. The system needs to turn that file into information that can be validated, searched, and reviewed.

I designed the processing workflow around the following stages:

Upload → Classification → Information Extraction → Validation → Indexing → Human Review → Approval or Rejection

Step 1: Document upload

Users upload supported PDF, JPG, or PNG documents. The backend validates the file type and size before processing it.

The original document is stored in AWS S3, while the application's database maintains the associated metadata and workflow state.

Step 2: Classification and extraction

The AI processing layer identifies the document category and extracts relevant fields into a structured representation.

For example, an invoice may contain:

  • Invoice number
  • Vendor name
  • Invoice date
  • Total amount
  • Payment-related details

Structured output makes it easier for downstream application logic to validate and use the information.

Step 3: Validation guardrails

LLM output should not automatically be treated as correct.

The validation layer checks whether the extracted information satisfies the application's requirements. Invalid or incomplete data can be flagged for additional review rather than silently passing through the workflow.

This distinction is important: an AI model can interpret information, but application rules must determine whether that information is acceptable.

Step 4: Human review

After processing, the document can enter a pending-review state.

Managers can inspect the extracted information and supporting document before approving or rejecting it. This creates a clear boundary between AI-assisted preparation and human authorization.

2. Why I Used LangGraph for Agentic Workflows

A document workflow is not always a simple sequence of LLM calls. Different outcomes may require different actions.

For example, a document with missing information should not follow exactly the same path as a document that has passed every validation check.

LangGraph helps represent this kind of process as a stateful graph, where nodes perform operations and edges determine what happens next.

In this project, the workflow separates responsibilities such as:

  • Document processing
  • Validation
  • Content indexing
  • Review scheduling
  • Human approval

This makes the workflow easier to understand and extend than placing every operation inside one large function.

It also provides a foundation for conditional routing, error handling, and human-in-the-loop interruptions.

One important design principle guided this implementation: agentic workflows should have clearly defined responsibilities and controlled transitions, not unrestricted autonomy.

3. Building a Document-Specific RAG Assistant

One of the most useful features is the AI assistant that answers questions about an uploaded document.

A general-purpose language model may generate a plausible answer without knowing the contents of a particular invoice or contract. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this limitation by retrieving relevant document content before generating an answer.

Here's how the retrieval pipeline works:

  1. Extract text from the uploaded document.
  2. Split the text into manageable chunks.
  3. Generate embeddings for those chunks.
  4. Store the vectors and associated metadata in ChromaDB.
  5. Convert a user's question into a retrieval query.
  6. Retrieve relevant document chunks.
  7. Provide the retrieved context to the language model to generate an answer.

For example, a user might ask:

“What is the total amount on this invoice, and which vendor issued it?”

Rather than relying only on the model's general knowledge, the assistant retrieves relevant information from the selected document and uses it to formulate the response.

Why document-specific retrieval matters

The assistant is designed to answer questions within the context of the selected document. This helps reduce irrelevant retrieval and makes responses more useful for document analysis.

It is also important to recognize that RAG does not eliminate hallucinations. Retrieval quality, source relevance, prompt design, and output validation all influence answer reliability.

For a production-ready implementation, I would further strengthen the assistant with explicit source citations, retrieval confidence checks, and tests for unsupported answers.

4. Keeping Humans in the Loop

Automation is valuable, but business workflows often require accountability.

Consider an invoice with an unexpected total or incomplete vendor information. Automatically approving it because an AI model returned a confident answer would introduce unnecessary risk.

The platform therefore separates the processing result from the approval decision.

  • The AI prepares and validates information.
  • The application maintains the document's workflow status.
  • The manager reviews the document.
  • The manager makes the approval or rejection decision.
  • The system records relevant lifecycle and audit information.

This design supports transparency and makes it easier to understand what happened to a document throughout its lifecycle.

Human review is not merely an additional screen in the application. It is an architectural control over how AI-generated information becomes an operational decision.

🔗 5. Connecting AI Workflows to External Tools with MCP

AI applications become more useful when they can interact with tools beyond the language model itself.

I integrated the Model Context Protocol (MCP) with Google Calendar to support scheduling approval reviews.

The workflow connects document processing with a real-world follow-up action: when a review needs to be scheduled, the application can use the calendar integration to create an event.

This demonstrates how an AI-enabled workflow can go beyond generating text and coordinate with an external service.

However, tool integration also introduces responsibilities around authorization, input validation, failure handling, and duplicate actions. These need to be handled carefully when expanding the integration.

6. Security, Storage, and Application Architecture

AI capabilities are only one part of a reliable document platform. The surrounding application needs to manage access, data, and workflow state correctly.

Authentication and role-based access control

I implemented secure authentication and role-based access control for administrators, managers, and employees.

Permissions determine which document operations are available to different roles. This is particularly important when documents contain business or financial information.

Database and file storage

PostgreSQL stores structured application data, with SQLAlchemy providing the ORM layer. AWS S3 handles persistent document storage.

Separating file storage from relational metadata makes the responsibilities of each component clearer.

Docker

Docker provides a consistent containerized setup, helping reduce differences between development and deployment environments.

These infrastructure decisions complement the AI workflow by giving the application a foundation for data persistence, access management, and maintainability.

7. Engineering Lessons and Trade-Offs

Building this project reinforced several important lessons about AI application development.

1. Structured output is not the same as validated output.

A model can return correctly formatted JSON while still producing incorrect values. Schema validation and business rules remain essential.

2. Retrieval quality matters as much as generation quality.

A strong language model cannot reliably answer a document-specific question if the relevant content was not retrieved. Chunking, embeddings, metadata, and retrieval strategy all influence the result.

3. Workflow state deserves explicit design.

Document statuses and approval transitions should be managed consistently. AI processing, database updates, and external tool calls should not be treated as one indivisible operation.

4. Automation should be proportional to risk.

Classification and information extraction are good candidates for automation. High-impact business approvals often benefit from human authorization.

5. Integrations create failure scenarios.

Storage operations, database transactions, model calls, and calendar events can fail independently. Retry policies, clear error states, and idempotent operations are important considerations as a system grows.

These lessons apply far beyond document processing. They are relevant to AI-powered support systems, compliance workflows, enterprise search, and other applications that combine probabilistic models with deterministic business logic.

What's Next?

There are several directions in which I would like to evolve the platform:

  • Improve extraction evaluation with representative test documents and field-level accuracy metrics.
  • Add stronger source citations and confidence-aware handling to document question answering.
  • Expand workflow observability with structured logs, execution traces, and failure metrics.
  • Introduce more comprehensive automated tests for permissions, approval transitions, and AI outputs.
  • Add asynchronous processing for larger document workloads.
  • Strengthen security with more granular authorization, retention policies, and audit controls.

The next stage is not simply adding more AI features. It is measuring reliability and making the existing workflow more robust.



Final Thoughts

Building this platform helped me explore how modern AI components can work together inside a practical software application.

LangChain and LangGraph provide building blocks for AI integration and stateful workflows. RAG connects language-model responses to document content. MCP enables interaction with external tools. Meanwhile, authentication, authorization, validation, storage, and audit logging provide the application-level controls needed around those capabilities.

The most important takeaway is that building a useful AI application requires more than connecting an LLM to an API. It requires designing the complete system around data quality, workflow state, security, and human accountability.

This project represents my continued exploration of AI engineering: moving beyond isolated model experiments and building applications that integrate AI into real software workflows.

I'd love to hear from other developers:

When building AI-powered business applications, where do you draw the line between autonomous processing and mandatory human approval?

title: Was the model unsure, or did the API call fail?
summary:
In an LLM application, seeing UNCERTAIN doesn't necessarily mean the model was unsure.

Sometimes the provider call failed entirely. If your application treats both cases the same way, you can end up debugging prompts and confidence thresholds when the real problem is an API key, a model name, or a network issue.

Reproduce the difference without an API key

You don't need a provider SDK or real credentials to see the distinction. This small example simulates a failed call and a model response that doesn't pass the confidence check.

Requires boothpy >= 0.5.4.

import booth

def dead(prompt):
    raise RuntimeError("401: invalid API key")

def unsure(prompt):
    return '{"answer": "Paris", "confidence": 0.2}'

a = booth.check(dead, "What is the capital of France?")
b = booth.check(unsure, "What is the capital of France?")

print(a.status, a.answer, a.call_failed, len(a.attempts))
# UNCERTAIN None True 2

print(b.status, b.answer, b.call_failed)
# UNCERTAIN Paris False

Both checks return UNCERTAIN, but for different reasons.

In the first case, the call fails. With the default max_retries=1, BOOTH makes two attempts. Neither reaches a usable response, so the result has no answer and call_failed is True.

In the second case, the call returns a response, but its confidence is too low for the checkpoint to accept it. The answer is available, and call_failed is False.

That distinction matters: retrying a request with an invalid API key costs another call without fixing the credential.

What call_failed actually tells you

BOOTH added result.call_failed in v0.5.4. It's also present in v0.5.6.

One detail matters: result.call_failed is True only when every attempt was a call failure.

Imagine the first attempt returns an uncertain response, and the retry then hits an unavailable provider. The overall result's call_failed can still be False, because not every attempt failed at the call level. To inspect the last attempt specifically, check:

last_attempt = result.attempts[-1]

if last_attempt.call_failed:
    print("The latest call failed:", last_attempt.error)

Log call failures, not every attempt error

BOOTH also provides an on_attempt callback. Be careful about which field you check: attempt.error can be populated for parsing failures too, such as a response where no valid JSON object was found. An error value alone doesn't prove that the provider call failed.

Check attempt.call_failed instead:

def log_attempt(index, attempt):
    if attempt.call_failed:
        print(
            f"Attempt {index + 1}: "
            f"the call itself failed: {attempt.error}"
        )

result = booth.check(
    call_llm,
    "What is the capital of France?",
    on_attempt=log_attempt,
)

For a simpler debugging path, you don't need a callback at all. After the check, inspect the last attempt:

if result.attempts and result.attempts[-1].error:
    print(result.attempts[-1].error)

That gives you the latest attempt's error message when one is available. Remember that it can describe a parsing failure as well as a call failure.

There's another limitation worth knowing: a call failure can still produce result.method == "parse_failure", the same method label that can appear when a model returns unusable output. Don't use method to distinguish provider failures from bad model output. Use the call-failure flags instead.

This came from a real integration issue

In an LLM application, seeing UNCERTAIN doesn't necessarily mean the model was unsure.

Sometimes the provider call failed entirely. If your application treats both cases the same way, you can end up debugging prompts and confidence thresholds when the real problem is an API key, a model name, or a network issue.

import booth

    raise RuntimeError("401: invalid API key")

    return '{"answer": "Paris", "confidence": 0.2}'

title: Three settings that decide whether EmbeddingGemma 2 search works on your GPU
summary:
EmbeddingGemma 2 is an embedding model Google DeepMind released on 6 October under Apache 2.0. An embedding model turns an input into a list of numbers (768 here) so that similar meanings get nearby lists, and search becomes "find the nearest list". This one takes text, images, video and audio into the same space, from a 1.5 GB download of 740M parameters.

We served it on a 16 GB NVIDIA RTX 2000 Ada on our own cloud. Loading it was easy. Three settings decided whether the vectors were correct and latency reasonable, so settle them before you write the indexing job.

The number format that fails without an error

GPUs can store numbers in compact 16-bit formats, float16 and bfloat16, to halve memory. Google's model card (the documentation shipped with the weights) allows only bfloat16 or float32. In float16, some values inside the network get too large to represent, and the card says you get NaN or subtly degraded embeddings with no exception. In a search index that means no crash, just worse rankings.

The card's suggested selection fits in one line:

# never float16: NaN or quietly wrong vectors, no exception
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported() else torch.float32

On a GPU without native bfloat16, the float32 fallback needs twice the memory. All our runs used a safe format, so the float16 failure is Google's warning, not something we reproduced. That run is our next test. Log which dtype your stack actually loads.

Photos were slow because the container saw 64 cores

Our first backend handled images two to five times slower than it should have. A profiler showed about 72 ms of GPU work per image against 0.33 to 0.44 seconds of CPU preprocessing. The container's CPU quota (the share of the host's processors it may use, set through Linux cgroups) was about 7 cores, but PyTorch counted the host's 64 and started 64 threads to fight over 7.

Limiting threads to the quota took a single image from 531 to 111 ms, eight images from 4,333 to 867 ms, and a 6-second video clip from 754 to 307 ms. Text and audio stayed almost flat, so a text-only benchmark never shows this.

Our example backend derives the thread count from the cgroup quota. Without a quota, you set it by hand. We verified this on one container only, so time CPU preprocessing and GPU encoding separately, per input type, on yours.

Freed GPU memory stays reserved

The complete model occupied 1.4 GB of GPU memory, or 0.5 GB with only the text part loaded. Single-input requests peaked at 2.6 GB. Batching is where it grows: eight documents of roughly 6,000 tokens each (a token is about a word or part of one) in one request peaked near 10 GB.

The surprise came afterwards. PyTorch caches released GPU memory for reuse, so the process held 11.6 GB until a restart. Calling torch.cuda.empty_cache() after very large requests fixed it: the same batch now leaves the process at 1.6 GB. For bulk indexing, size the GPU for your biggest batch.

Shorter vectors: same speed, some quality loss

Google trained the model with Matryoshka Representation Learning, so the first 512, 256 or 128 numbers of each vector work as a smaller embedding. Truncating was not faster for us (34 to 35 ms per query at every size). Only storage and payload shrink.

The quality cost depends on the input type, per the model card:

Benchmark 768 256 128
MTEB multilingual v2 (text) 61.36 60.41 57.89
MMEB v2 (images and video) 59.01 56.24 45.65
MSEB retrieval (speech) 69.54 66.76 56.71

The card calls 256 close to lossless. At 128, text holds, but image and video search drops by almost a quarter, so the card keeps 128 for text. Re-normalize each vector after cutting it (scale it back to length 1), and embed queries and documents at the same size. Our EmbeddingGemma 2 measurements of VRAM and latency per input type show what each option costs on a 16 GB card.

What the search test does and does not show

Our test index had twelve files and zero text: photos, short videos and spoken recordings. Six English queries each ranked the correct file first. "How to knead bread dough" matched a Spanish recording of a bread recipe. We generated all twelve files, so this confirms the cross-modal pipeline runs end to end, not how the model compares with others. The images came from Sperid Labs' Iris-3B, which we ran in an earlier test of the Iris-3B image model, and the voices from Pocket TTS.

On serving: vLLM, the open-source inference server, did not support this model in version 0.31.0 when we checked, not even for text, so we wrote a small Python backend on sentence-transformers. Google's launch post names vLLM, SGLang, Ollama and llama.cpp as supported tooling, so check current versions first. The complete EmbeddingGemma 2 deployment write-up, with latency and VRAM tables for every input type, covers the request format, start-up times and all five problems we ran into.

Credits

Google DeepMind built EmbeddingGemma 2: the model, its image, video and audio components, the benchmark results and the float16 warning. Sahil Dua and Henrique Schechter Vera wrote the launch post. The truncatable vectors rely on Matryoshka Representation Learning by Kusupati and colleagues. Hugging Face transformers supports the model from version 5.19.0, and sentence-transformers runs it. PyAV decoded our audio and video, and ffmpeg cut the clips. We wrote the backend, took the measurements and fixed the thread count and the memory cache.

The backend code, the SDK example and every number above are in the EmbeddingGemma 2 deployment article on inferencekey.com.

title: 6 of 40 sites were pointing Google at a sitemap URL that returns HTML
summary:
A robots.txt Sitemap line that resolves to 200 is not the same thing as a readable sitemap. I found out the expensive way, on six sites at once, and the bug had been live for months.

The failure mode: 200 + text/html 

$ curl -sI https://example.com/sitemap.xml.gz
HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8

That is the entire bug, and it is completely invisible to normal monitoring.

The chain is boring and extremely common:

  1. The site was originally built with a generator that gzipped its sitemap, so robots.txt got Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml.gz.
  2. The build changed (Hugo out, a SPA build in). The .gz file stopped being produced.
  3. The web server has the standard single-page-app fallback: 
location / {
    try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
}
  1. A request for a file that no longer exists therefore returns 200 OK with the app shell as HTML.

The crawler asks for a sitemap, gets a web page, and gives up. Silently. No 404 in the access log to alert on, no error in the build, and the submit button in Search Console still says "Success".

Six of the forty sites I look after had this exact robots.txt line. Every one of them returned a green 200.

Why status-code monitoring never catches it

  • A synthetic check that asserts status == 200 passes.
  • An uptime monitor passes.
  • A "sitemap submitted successfully" message in Search Console passes — submission is just a queue write.
  • Even a page-level error tracker passes, because nothing errored.

The only thing that noticed was Search Console URL Inspection, which reported entire sites as unknown to Google. That looks like an authority problem, so the first instinct is to buy links. That would have been money spent on the wrong problem: the discovery channel itself was broken.

Check 1 — parse the sitemap, don't fetch it

Never assert on the status code alone. Assert that the bytes parse as XML.

import re, urllib.request, xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

UA = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; sitemap-audit/1.0)"}

def sitemaps_from_robots(host):
    req = urllib.request.Request(f"https://{host}/robots.txt", headers=UA)
    txt = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20).read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
    return re.findall(r"(?im)^\s*sitemap:\s*(\S+)", txt)

def assert_real_sitemap(url):
    r = urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers=UA), timeout=30)
    body = r.read()
    ctype = r.headers.get("content-type", "")
    if "xml" not in ctype:
        raise AssertionError(f"{url}: wrong content-type {ctype!r} ({len(body)} bytes)")
    try:
        root = ET.fromstring(body)
    except ET.ParseError as e:
        raise AssertionError(f"{url}: not XML — {e}; first bytes {body[:80]!r}")
    return root

Two details matter here:

  • content-type is a cheap early exit, but it is not sufficient. I have seen application/xml served for an error page.
  • ET.fromstring is the real assertion. "The string starts with <" passes for , which is precisely the case we are trying to catch.

Six sites, six failures, thirty seconds of runtime. That one function was worth more than every link-building experiment I ran that quarter.

Check 2 — a sitemap full of soft 404s

Fixing the .gz path made the sitemap readable, and immediately exposed a second layer: the SPA fallback means any URL returns 200. So a sitemap can list thousands of URLs that are not files, do not correspond to a route, and render the generic shell.

Mine had 385 entries. 188 of them were fake.

The tell is that a soft 404 renders identical content to the fallback. So compare a fingerprint, not a status:

import hashlib, re

def fingerprint(html):
    m = re.search(r"]*>(.*?)", html, re.S | re.I)
    return hashlib.sha1((m.group(1) if m else "").encode()).hexdigest()

shell = fingerprint(open("index.html").read())

for loc in sitemap_locs:
    body = urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(loc, headers=UA)).read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
    if fingerprint(body) == shell:
        print("SOFT-404:", loc)

For a pre-rendered site it is stricter: each route should have its own </code>, so equal titles means the route was not actually pre-rendered.</p> <p>Result after pruning: 385 → 197 entries, all of which resolve to a distinct page.</p> <h2> Check 3 — wherever <code>canonical</code> points, that URL must return 200 </h2> <p>This one I consider the most dangerous class of bug, because it does not look like a bug at all.</p> <p>A page declared <code><link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/en/"></code>. title: Keeping Your Streamlit App Awake with Serverless Functions and a Free Cron Job
summary:
You deploy a little Streamlit app on Community Cloud, share the link, and a day later it's showing a sleepy "Zzzz, this app has gone to sleep due to inactivity" page. Anyone who opens it has to click a button and wait for a cold start.

There's no keep-alive switch in Streamlit Community Cloud, and the advice on the forums boils down to "push an empty commit" or "automate a browser". Both work, but both are heavier than they need to be. There's a simpler way: do exactly what that button does, with one HTTP request, on a schedule.

⚠️ This uses an undocumented endpoint that the Streamlit web page itself calls. It can change without notice. Only use it on apps you own, and keep the schedule gentle.

What the "wake up" button really does

If you open dev tools on a sleeping app and click Yes, get this app back up!, you'll see a single request:

POST https://.streamlit.app/api/v2/app/resume

It needs two small things besides the POST itself, and neither one is a login:

  1. A CSRF token. The page never stores it anywhere fancy. It simply remembers the x-csrf-token response header from the previous API call and sends it back. The server also sets a matching _streamlit_csrf cookie on that same response.
  2. A machine id. A random UUID sent as x-streamlit-machine-id.

So the whole dance is: ask for the app status, grab the token and cookie, then POST to resume.

Try it with curl

I'm using webpie.streamlit.app here, swap in your own app URL. Save this as wake.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Wake a sleeping Streamlit Community Cloud app.
# Usage: ./wake.sh https://webpie.streamlit.app
set -euo pipefail

APP_URL="${1:?usage: ./wake.sh https://webpie.streamlit.app}"
COOKIES="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$COOKIES"' EXIT

# Step 1: any API call hands us a CSRF cookie (saved in the jar)
# and an x-csrf-token response header (we grab it here).
CSRF_TOKEN=$(
  curl --silent --output /dev/null --dump-header - \
    --cookie-jar "$COOKIES" \
    "$APP_URL/api/v2/app/status" \
  | tr -d '\r' \
  | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1) == "x-csrf-token" { print $2 }'
)

# Step 2: the browser also sends a random UUID as a machine id.
MACHINE_ID=$(uuidgen | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')

# Step 3: this is the call behind the "Yes, get this app back up!" button.
curl --silent --include --request POST \
  --cookie "$COOKIES" --cookie-jar "$COOKIES" \
  --header "x-csrf-token: $CSRF_TOKEN" \
  --header "x-streamlit-machine-id: $MACHINE_ID" \
  --header "origin: $APP_URL" \
  --header "referer: $APP_URL/" \
  "$APP_URL/api/v2/app/resume"
echo

# Step 4 (optional): check the status afterwards
curl --silent --cookie "$COOKIES" "$APP_URL/api/v2/app/status"
echo

Run it:

chmod +x wake.sh
./wake.sh https://webpie.streamlit.app

A 204 No Content from the resume call means the request was accepted. The status call at the end shows the app's state; while it's booting, the status number changes. (An app that's already awake just answers normally, so it's safe to run any time.)

Make it run itself

A shell script on your laptop doesn't help while you're asleep too. The nice part is that the logic is just fetch calls, so it runs on almost any serverless platform: Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Netlify, AWS Lambda, Deno Deploy. Pick whichever you already use.

Here's the core logic once, in plain JavaScript:

// Shared logic: wake a Streamlit Community Cloud app.
// Works in Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Netlify, Node 18+, anything with fetch.
export async function wakeApp(appUrl) {
  // Step 1: any API call gives us a CSRF cookie and an x-csrf-token header.
  const status = await fetch(`${appUrl}/api/v2/app/status`);
  const csrfToken = status.headers.get("x-csrf-token");
  const cookies = status.headers
    .getSetCookie()
    .map((cookie) => cookie.split(";")[0]) // keep "name=value", drop attributes
    .join("; ");

  // Step 2: this is the call behind the "Yes, get this app back up!" button.
  const resume = await fetch(`${appUrl}/api/v2/app/resume`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      cookie: cookies,
      "x-csrf-token": csrfToken,
      "x-streamlit-machine-id": crypto.randomUUID(),
      origin: appUrl,
      referer: `${appUrl}/`,
    },
  });

  return { ok: resume.ok, status: resume.status };
}

Option A: Cloudflare Workers

worker.js:

import { wakeApp } from "./wake.js";

export default {
  async fetch(request, env) {
    // Optional: stop strangers from poking your endpoint
    const secret = new URL(request.url).searchParams.get("key");
    if (env.WAKE_KEY && secret !== env.WAKE_KEY) {
      return new Response("Nope", { status: 401 });
    }

    const result = await wakeApp(env.APP_URL);
    return Response.json(result);
  },
};

Set APP_URL (for example https://webpie.streamlit.app) and an optional WAKE_KEY as variables in the Worker settings, then deploy with npx wrangler deploy. You'll get a URL like https://wake-streamlit..workers.dev/?key=.

Option B: Vercel

Put wake.js in your project root and add api/wake.js:

import { wakeApp } from "../wake.js";

export default async function handler(req, res) {
  if (process.env.WAKE_KEY && req.query.key !== process.env.WAKE_KEY) {
    return res.status(401).send("Nope");
  }

  const result = await wakeApp(process.env.APP_URL);
  res.status(200).json(result);
}

Add APP_URL and WAKE_KEY under Project Settings → Environment Variables and deploy. Your endpoint is https://.vercel.app/api/wake?key=.

Trigger it with cron-job.org (free)

You don't even need the platform's own scheduler. cron-job.org is free and will call any URL on a schedule:

  1. Create an account and click Create cronjob.
  2. URL: the Worker or Vercel endpoint from above, including ?key=....
  3. Schedule: every 6 hours is plenty. Apps seem to sleep after roughly 12 hours without visitors, so you want to land well inside that window.
  4. Save. Under the job's history you can see each run's status code. 200 means your function ran.

That's the whole setup: cron-job.org pokes your serverless function, the function pokes Streamlit, and your app stays warm. No browser, no Selenium, no fake commits.

Things worth knowing

  • It's unofficial. If Streamlit changes the endpoint, the script breaks. Check the cron history now and then.
  • It's polite use only. One request every few hours for your own app. Please don't hammer it.
  • Waking isn't the same as being busy. This resumes a sleeping app. It doesn't pretend to be traffic, so the app can still go back to sleep later, which is why the schedule keeps repeating.
  • Keep the key secret so nobody else can trigger your function.

If you'd rather stay inside the official lines, the alternative is hosting the app somewhere that doesn't sleep. But for a free-tier hobby app, a 20-line function and a free cron service is hard to beat.

Happy hacking!

Happy hacking!

title: One Trip.com URL, Five Pulls, Twelve Hours: 21 Different Hotels, Six Every Time
summary:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them reads Trip.com: a city, two dates and a guest count in, one row per hotel out, with the live nightly rate for exactly those dates.

Trip.com is the booking channel for most of Asia and it has no public web API, so a scraper is the only way in. The field I expected to cause trouble was the price. It didn't. What caused trouble was something I hadn't thought to check: which hotels the page shows you at all.

The same URL, five times, one day

My QA runs hit a hardcoded list URL so I can diff the output day over day. On 21 October 2026 five of them fired against a byte-identical URL:

https://www.trip.com/hotels/list?city=723&checkin=2026%2F11%2F20
  &checkout=2026%2F11%2F23&adult=2&children=0&curr=USD&locale=en-XX

Bali, three nights, two adults, USD. Pulls at 00:30, 07:48, 07:55, 08:20 and 12:10 — an 11-hour-40-minute span. Twelve hotel rows each, which is one page, 60 rows total.

Those 60 rows contained 21 distinct hotels. Six appeared in all five pulls. Nine appeared exactly once.

Appeared in Hotels Median nightly
5 of 5 pulls 6 $22
4 of 5 3 $30
3 of 5 3 $89
1 of 5 9 $52

Pairwise, the overlap decays with the gap between requests, and it decays cleanly:

Pair Gap Common rows
07:55 vs 08:20 25 min 12 / 12
07:48 vs 07:55 7 min 11 / 12
00:30 vs 07:48 7 h 8 / 12
08:20 vs 12:10 4 h 8 / 12
07:48 vs 12:10 4 h 7 / 12
00:30 vs 12:10 11 h 40 6 / 12

So this is not per-request randomness. Requests minutes apart come back identical or off by one row. Requests hours apart come back half different. That is the signature of a result set that is assembled and cached, then reassembled later — not a ranking you can treat as stable.

It replicates. Three pulls on 20 October against the 19–22 November window: the two fired a minute apart agreed 12 of 12, the one twenty hours earlier agreed 7 of 12 with both. Two pulls this morning, four hours apart, agreed 7 of 12 — a $260 Kempinski vanished, a $283 resort appeared.

What that does to a number you'd actually report

The prices held almost perfectly still. Across the six hotels present in all five pulls, the nightly rate moved in three of them, by exactly one dollar: $34→$35, $10→$11, $28→$27. Kenran Resort sat at $72 in all five, Moonloka at $16. If you track one named property, Trip.com is boringly consistent and this article is irrelevant to you.

Aggregate those same five pulls and the stillness disappears:

Pull Median nightly Mean nightly
00:30 $31.00 $51.60
07:48 $35.00 $62.80
07:55 $31.50 $61.40
08:20 $31.50 $61.30
12:10 $23.50 $39.00

The mean nightly rate for Bali swung from $39.00 to $62.80 — a 61% spread — on one day, from one URL, with essentially no price changing. Every dollar of that swing is sampling. The 12:10 pull happened to miss the expensive tail: no Anvaya at $110, no Kayon Jungle at $281, no ARNA at $90. The 07:48 pull caught all three.

Which direction it biases is not random either. The six properties that never moved are all in the cheap half — $9 to $72, median $22. The nine one-time visitors have a median of $52 and include $86, $98, $106 and $166. Page one has a sticky cheap core and a rotating expensive tail, and a "city average" built on page one inherits whichever part of that tail it happened to catch.

Asking for more rows is a different question, not a bigger answer

The obvious fix is to pull deeper. It works, but not in the way "more data, same answer" suggests. Three runs on Bangkok this morning, 21–24 November, same two adults, minutes apart:

  • 12 rows: median $38.50, mean $45.10
  • a second 12-row run three minutes later: 11 of 12 the same hotels, zero price differences, order reshuffled
  • 48 rows, thirty seconds after that: 48 distinct properties, median $53.50, mean $75.30

Median $38.50 against $53.50 on the same city, the same dates, the same minute. Page one is not a random sample — it is cheap-skewed, and each extra page walks you up the price distribution. The 48-row run also did not contain 2 of the 12 hotels the first run had just returned.

The practical rule I now use: if you want a city-level statistic, fix the row count and never compare two samples of different depth. If you want coverage, run it more than once and union on hotelId — the churn is working for you then, because five pulls of 12 gave me 21 properties, not 12.

import requests, statistics
from collections import defaultdict

TOKEN = ""
seen = defaultdict(dict)

for _ in range(5):  # five pulls, spaced hours apart by a scheduler
    rows = requests.post(
        "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~tripcom-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items",
        params={"token": TOKEN},
        json={"cityId": 723, "cityName": "Bali",
              "checkIn": "2026-11-21", "checkOut": "2026-11-24",
              "adults": 2, "maxHotels": 48, "currency": "USD"},
    ).json()
    for r in rows:
        if r.get("type") == "hotel" and r.get("price"):
            seen[r["hotelId"]] = r          # last write wins, one row per property

print(len(seen), "distinct hotels")
print("median", statistics.median(r["price"] for r in seen.values()))

Note the type == "hotel" filter. The last row of every run is a free notice row with the run's own accounting — rowsDelivered, chargedTotalUsd, timings. The 48-row Bangkok run reports {"rowsDelivered": 48, "chargedTotalUsd": 0.144} and finished in 28 seconds. Leave it in your dataframe and it becomes a hotel with no price.

Two price fields you should not multiply

While I had 451 priced rows from 22 runs sitting on disk, I checked the arithmetic between price (nightly) and totalPrice (the stay).

totalPrice was larger than price × nights in 451 of 451 rows. Median ratio 1.200, range 1.056 to 1.339. Two things are stacked in there: totalPrice is the number Trip.com prints as incl. taxes & fees, and price is rounded to a whole currency unit, which on a $9 room is an 11% rounding step on its own. I am not going to tell you the tax rate, because Trip.com ships a formatted total and a rounded nightly figure and splitting them is guessing. What I will say is that price * nights is never the number the guest pays, and the error is a fifth, not a rounding wobble.

The discount badges have a smaller version of the same gap. 373 rows carried an originalPrice, and it was above price in all 373 — median implied discount 29.4%. On the 364 rows that also carried an "N% off" tag in dealTags, the discount you compute from the two numbers beat the badge in 341 of them, median by 2.7 points: Lloyd's Inn says 61% off with $80 → $28 next to it, which is 65%. Use the badge as a label and compute your own number, and don't expect them to agree to the point.

The Actor is Trip.com Scraper — hotel cards with the live rate for your dates, property details, and the guest reviews off the hotel page, by city ID or by URL.

When this is the wrong tool

  • You need a booking. This reads public pages. There is no availability hold, no rate code and no reservation here.
  • You need every hotel in a city, exactly once. You will get there by unioning repeated runs, not by one run. If you need a guaranteed complete inventory as of a timestamp, Trip.com's page one will not give you one.
  • You need per-room rate plans. Each row carries the one room Trip.com chose to price for your dates — roomName, roomId — not the hotel's full rate table.
  • You need a tax breakdown. You get the pre-tax nightly figure and the all-in total. The split between them is not published as fields, and I'd rather ship two honest numbers than three invented ones.

If you keep one thing from this: before you trust a scraped ranking, pull it twice an hour apart and count the overlap. A field that disagrees with itself is obvious. A row set that quietly swaps half its members is not, and it moves your averages far harder than any price ever will.

title: How to Track SEC EDGAR Filings as JSON (Without Maintaining a Scraper)
summary:
How to Track SEC EDGAR Filings as JSON (Without Maintaining a Scraper)

If you are building filing alerts, compliance checks or equity-research workflows, SEC EDGAR is the
source: every filing from every US issuer, published minutes after acceptance. The official EDGAR
APIs are free and return JSON — but wiring them up yourself still means declaring a User-Agent the
SEC accepts, staying under its published limit of 10 requests per second, paginating full-text
search results, and handling fields that one endpoint returns while another does not.

Here is how to get the data in two ways, with a real sample of the output.

The official API, in a nutshell

  • Endpoints: the EDGAR application programming interfaces (submissions by CIK, filing metadata, full-text search).
  • No API key: EDGAR's endpoints are anonymous.
  • Politeness rules: send a declared User-Agent with your contact information and stay under the published limit of 10 requests per second; requests that ignore this are rejected.
  • Scope: filing metadata and issuer organisations only. There is no officer or contact data here — personal data stays out of scope, by design.

Option A — call the official API directly 

curl -sS -A "your-app your@email.com" \
  "https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000320193.json" | jq '.filings.recent | .accessionNumber[0:3]'

That works fine for one issuer. The moment you watch a shortlist of companies or run a full-text
search, you are maintaining pagination, date filtering and field reconciliation for every endpoint
you touch.

Option B — run a ready-made Actor

steadfetch/sec-edgar-monitor wraps those endpoints on the Apify platform: it handles the declared
User-Agent, the 10 req/s budget, pagination, retries and an output schema check on every run. No SEC
key needed (an optional proxy of your own token keeps your run budget isolated).

Input — by issuer, or by full-text query:

{ "cik": "0000320193", "formTypes": ["10-K", "10-Q", "8-K"], "startDate": "2026-01-01", "maxResults": 10 }

{ "query": "supply agreement", "startDate": "2026-10-01", "endDate": "2026-10-17", "maxResults": 25 }

At least one of cik or query is required.

Run it with one API call:

curl -sS -X POST \
  "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/steadfetch~sec-edgar-monitor/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"cik":"0000320193","formTypes":["10-Q"],"startDate":"2026-07-01","maxResults":5}'

Real output sample (a genuine filing record, as published in the Actor's docs):

{
    "accession_no": "0000320193-26-000020",
    "cik": "0000320193",
    "company_name": "Apple Inc.",
    "form_type": "10-Q",
    "filing_date": "2026-07-31",
    "report_date": "2026-06-27",
    "acceptance_datetime": "2026-07-31T14:01:02.000Z",
    "primary_document_url": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019326000020/aapl-20260627.htm",
    "is_amendment": false,
    "url": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019326000020/aapl-20260627.htm",
    "scrapedAt": "2026-10-19T12:00:00.000Z"
}

One dataset item per filing, validated against the published dataset schema on every run — if a field
type changes upstream, the run fails loudly instead of writing bad rows.

JavaScript and Python

Node.js, with apify-client:

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: process.env.APIFY_TOKEN });

const { defaultDatasetId } = await client.actor('steadfetch/sec-edgar-monitor').call({
  cik: '0000320193',
  formTypes: ['10-K', '10-Q', '8-K'],
  startDate: '2026-01-01',
  maxResults: 10,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(defaultDatasetId).listItems();
console.log(JSON.stringify(items, null, 2));

Python, with apify-client:

import json, os
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run = client.actor("steadfetch/sec-edgar-monitor").call(run_input={
    "cik": "0000320193", "formTypes": ["10-K", "10-Q", "8-K"],
    "startDate": "2026-01-01", "maxResults": 10,
})
items = client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).list_items().items
print(json.dumps(items, indent=2))

Runnable versions of all three (curl, Node, Python) plus the sample output live in
steadfetch/examples/sec-edgar-monitor.

What it costs

Pay-per-result pricing on Apify: 5.00 USD per 1,000 filings (0.005 USD per filing) plus a
0.00005 USD run-start fee. Failed requests, retries and empty searches are not charged per result,
and no proxy is billed — EDGAR answers with structured JSON, so no browser is involved.

Fields you get

Field Meaning
accession_no Official accession number of the filing
cik / company_name Issuer identity
form_type 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, and the rest of the EDGAR form taxonomy
filing_date / report_date When it was filed and the period it covers
acceptance_datetime EDGAR acceptance timestamp — null when the full-text endpoint omits it; never invented
primary_document_url / url Direct link to the filing document
is_amendment Whether the filing amends an earlier one
scrapedAt Extraction timestamp, on every record

Getting started

Open the Actor page in the Apify Store, run it
from the console or with the API snippets above, and pull the dataset into whatever you already use.

only. More at apify.com/steadfetch.

title: Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration
summary:
Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration

Introduction

In this rapidly evolving era of Artificial Intelligence, I wanted to go beyond simply learning about AI and start understanding how it works in real-world applications. My goal is to dive deeper into the world of AI, explore its workflows, understand how Large Language Models (LLMs) operate, and learn how AI agents can reason, use tools, and solve practical problems.

As technology continues to advance, I believe the best way to grow as a developer is to challenge myself by building real-world applications, experimenting with new technologies, and learning from the problems I encounter along the way. I wanted to push my boundaries, strengthen my AI engineering skills, and contribute to the growing AI ecosystem through practical implementation.

That motivation led me to build AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration.

The idea was to create more than a traditional chatbot. I wanted to explore how an AI assistant could interact with external tools, retrieve relevant information, and respond to different user requests through a single conversational interface.

In this article, I'll share my journey of building this project, the technologies I explored, how tool integration works, the challenges involved, and the lessons I learned while developing my practical AI skills.

Project Links

Explore the project and its source code:

  • Live Demo: AI Chat Assistant
  • Frontend Repository: AI Chat Assistant Frontend
  • Backend Repository: AI Chat Assistant Backend

Feel free to explore the code, try the live application, and share your feedback. I'd love to hear your thoughts and suggestions!

1. The Problem: An AI Model Alone Is Not Enough

LLMs are powerful at understanding natural language, generating responses, summarizing content, and explaining technical concepts. However, a standalone model has limitations.

For example:

  • It may not know the latest news or current weather conditions.
  • Its training data may not include recent technical information.
  • It cannot automatically access external services without an integration.
  • It needs additional application logic to interact with APIs and handle errors.

I wanted to solve these limitations by building an assistant that could select the appropriate tools when answering different types of questions.

For example, when a user asks, "What is the weather in Chennai?", the assistant should use a weather service rather than simply generate an answer from its language model.

Similarly, when a user asks a programming question, it can use a relevant technical information source when appropriate.

This led me to explore agentic AI and tool calling.

2. What Is Agentic AI?

Agentic AI refers to AI systems that can work toward a goal by choosing actions, using tools, and incorporating the results into their responses.

A traditional chatbot typically follows a straightforward pattern:

User input → LLM → Response

An agentic assistant can follow a more flexible workflow:

User input → Understand the request → Select a tool → Execute the tool → Process the result → Generate a response

For example, consider this request:

"Find recent technology news and summarize the important points."

The assistant can identify that the user needs current information, invoke a news or search tool, process the returned results, and generate a concise summary.

The LLM handles language understanding and decision-making, while external tools provide capabilities that the model does not have on its own.

An important distinction is that the LLM does not magically gain access to external services. The application must explicitly provide the tools, their descriptions, and the code needed to execute them.

3. Project Architecture

I designed the application around a frontend, a backend API, an LLM integration, and a collection of specialized tools.

The main components are:

Frontend

The frontend provides the conversational interface where users submit questions and view assistant responses.

Backend API

The backend receives requests, manages the conversation flow, coordinates model interactions, executes tool calls, and returns the final response.

LLM integration

The language model interprets user requests, determines when a tool may be useful, and generates natural-language responses from the available context.

Tool integrations

Individual tools connect the assistant to external information sources and services, such as weather, news, web search, Wikipedia, movie information, Stack Overflow, and Notion.

Supporting services

The application also uses supporting infrastructure such as a database and Redis, depending on the feature and workflow, for data persistence and caching.

The overall flow looks like this:

              User
               |
               v
        Frontend Chat UI
               |
               v
          Backend API
               |
               v
          LLM / Agent
               |
        Selects a tool
               |
               v
       Tool Execution Layer
               |
       +-------+--------+
       |       |        |
     Weather  Search   News
       |       |        |
       +-------+--------+
               |
               v
        Tool Result
               |
               v
        LLM Generates
        Final Response
               |
               v
          Frontend UI

This architecture separates the user interface, orchestration logic, and external integrations, making the application easier to extend and maintain.

4. Integrating Multiple Tools

One of the most interesting parts of the project was connecting different capabilities through a single assistant.

Each tool has a specific responsibility.

Weather

The weather tool retrieves weather information for a requested location. This allows the assistant to answer questions that require current or forecast data.

Web Search

The web search tool helps retrieve information from online sources when a question requires information beyond the model's built-in knowledge.

News

The news integration provides access to recent news information, helping the assistant respond to requests about current events.

Wikipedia

Wikipedia provides reference information about people, places, organizations, and general topics.

Movie Information

The movie tool supports queries about films and related information, demonstrating how a specialized API can extend an assistant's capabilities.

Stack Overflow

This integration helps retrieve programming-related discussions and technical information that may be relevant to developer questions.

Notion

The Notion integration connects the assistant to a productivity and knowledge-management platform, where supported operations can help users work with information in their workspace.

The key idea is that these tools are not interchangeable. Each one has its own inputs, outputs, API requirements, and possible failure conditions.

The assistant needs enough information about each tool to select it appropriately.

5. How Tool Calling Works

A tool-enabled LLM workflow generally consists of several steps.

Step 1: Receive the request

The backend receives the user's message and prepares the relevant conversation context.

Step 2: Ask the model to determine the next action

The model evaluates the request and can return either a normal response or a structured tool call, depending on the framework and tool definitions.

Step 3: Execute the selected tool

The backend validates the requested arguments and calls the corresponding function or external API.

Step 4: Return the result to the model

The tool output is passed back into the conversation so the model can interpret it.

Step 5: Generate the final answer

The model converts the available information into a response that is understandable to the user.

Conceptually, a tool definition might look like this:

def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    """
    Retrieve weather information for a city.
    """
    # Call the configured weather API here.
    # Validate the response and handle API errors.
    return {
        "city": city,
        "temperature": 28,
        "condition": "Partly cloudy"
    }

This is a simplified example showing the shape of a tool function, not the complete implementation of a production weather integration.

In a real application, the function would retrieve actual weather data, validate the location, handle timeouts, and report errors appropriately.

The LLM should not invent tool results. It should base its answer on the returned information and communicate when reliable data is unavailable.

6. Technology Stack

The project combines frontend development, backend engineering, AI integration, and external services.

The main technologies include:

  • Next.js and React: Building the frontend experience.
  • FastAPI: Exposing backend endpoints and coordinating application logic.
  • Python: Implementing backend functionality and tool integrations.
  • LLM providers: Powering natural-language understanding, reasoning, and response generation.
  • LangChain and related agent tooling: Supporting model and tool integration where configured.
  • PostgreSQL: Providing relational data persistence.
  • Redis: Supporting caching and other appropriate fast-access operations.
  • External APIs: Providing specialized information and capabilities.

Each technology addresses a different part of the system. The frontend handles interaction, the backend coordinates execution, the model processes language, and external APIs provide information or actions.

The exact model, API provider, and available operations depend on the configured integrations.

7. Challenges I Had to Consider

Building an AI assistant involves more than connecting a model to an API. Several engineering concerns become important as the number of tools increases.

Choosing the right tool

Similar user requests can require different tools, and vague questions can be difficult to interpret.

Clear tool descriptions, well-defined parameters, and appropriate model instructions help improve tool selection.

Handling API failures

External services can return errors, enforce rate limits, or respond slowly.

The backend should handle timeouts, validate responses, and return useful error messages rather than allowing one failed integration to break the entire conversation.

Managing API keys

Third-party API credentials should remain on the server and be loaded through environment variables or a suitable secrets-management system.

They should never be exposed in frontend code or committed to a public repository.

Keeping responses grounded

When a question requires current information, the assistant should use the relevant external source instead of presenting unsupported information as fact.

It is also important to distinguish retrieved information from the model's own explanation.

Maintaining a modular architecture

Adding more tools can make backend logic difficult to maintain if every integration is implemented inside a single large function.

Separating tool implementations from orchestration makes it easier to add capabilities, test individual integrations, and handle failures independently.

These considerations helped me understand why reliable AI applications need thoughtful backend engineering in addition to a capable language model.

8. Security and Reliability Considerations

An AI assistant that can access external services needs appropriate safeguards.

Some important practices include:

  • Validate tool arguments before executing them.
  • Apply authentication and authorization to protected endpoints.
  • Use request timeouts and controlled retry policies.
  • Limit tool permissions to the operations the application actually needs.
  • Avoid passing secrets or unnecessary sensitive data into model prompts.
  • Sanitize external content and treat retrieved text as untrusted input.
  • Apply rate limits and usage controls where appropriate.
  • Log useful operational information without exposing credentials or private conversation content.

For integrations that can modify external data, such as creating or updating records, additional permission checks and confirmation steps may be necessary.

These controls help make tool-enabled AI systems safer and more predictable.

9. What I Learned

This project helped me understand how LLMs can become part of a complete software system rather than functioning as isolated text-generation components.

Some of my main takeaways were:

LLMs need reliable tools. A language model becomes more useful for current or specialized questions when it can access appropriate external information.

Backend design matters. Tool orchestration, validation, error handling, authentication, and API integration are essential parts of an AI application.

Modularity improves extensibility. Keeping integrations separate makes it easier to introduce new capabilities without rewriting the entire application.

AI responses need grounding. A polished response is not necessarily a correct one. Reliable results depend on tool quality, context, validation, and clear handling of uncertainty.

Full-stack development and AI engineering complement each other. Building a useful assistant requires frontend interaction, backend APIs, model integration, and operational reliability to work together.

10. What's Next?

There are several ways to improve a multi-tool assistant as it evolves:

  • Add streaming responses for a more interactive experience.
  • Improve conversation memory and context management.
  • Introduce retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for private or domain-specific knowledge.
  • Add structured evaluation to measure tool-selection accuracy.
  • Improve observability with tracing, latency metrics, and error monitoring.
  • Introduce more granular permissions for tools that can modify external data.
  • Explore standardized tool interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), where appropriate.

These improvements can help move an experimental AI assistant toward a more reliable and maintainable application.

Conclusion

Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration was an opportunity to explore the intersection of full-stack development and modern AI engineering.

The project demonstrates how a conversational interface, an LLM, a backend orchestration layer, and external tools can work together to answer different types of questions.

More importantly, it reinforced an important lesson: building a useful AI application is not just about choosing a powerful model. It is about designing the systems around that model so it can access reliable information, use tools appropriately, and communicate results clearly.

I'm continuing to explore LLM engineering, agentic workflows, and practical AI integrations, and I'm looking forward to applying these lessons to more complex projects.

If you're building an AI assistant yourself, I'd be interested to hear what tools you're integrating and what challenges you've encountered.

Thanks for reading!

title: Private Receipt Exports: Signed Download URLs and Per-Tenant Object Storage Layout
summary:
Use a private bucket per tenant and hand out short-lived signed download URLs. For a SaaS that generates private export files — scanned receipts, CSV extracts, PDF summaries — and lets a user fetch them later, that is the entire answer. No CDN, no file-serving service, no permanent links. Any S3-compatible object storage does this, so the vendor question matters far less than the layout question.

The layout question is where the tenant boundary lives.

Where the storage boundary sits in a receipt pipeline

The system I have in mind is a logistics back office. Drivers photograph fuel and toll receipts, a Python worker pushes each file into storage untouched, an extraction model reads amounts and vendor names out of it, and the finance team later opens a matched expense line and clicks through to the original scan. Auditors care about that last step more than anything else in the pipeline: the extracted JSON is a derived artifact, and the image is the evidence.

So the data flow is: bytes in, one row in Postgres holding tenant_id, bucket, key, checksum and extraction status, and — much later, maybe eighteen months later — a signed URL minted on demand when someone with the right tenant claim asks for the file.

That is the whole boundary. Storage's job begins when the bytes land and ends when the signed link expires.

It does not know what a tenant is. It cannot answer "every receipt from carrier X in March," because object listing filters by key prefix, not by metadata. Both of those facts push you toward the same design: encode tenancy in the bucket and prefix, and keep authorization, search and audit history in your own database where you can join them against everything else. I keep the checksum in that row too, since my eval harness re-scores extraction accuracy against the stored originals and I want a hard guarantee the bytes never drifted.

If you are already assembling a backend out of a dozen vendor dashboards, Infrai is worth trying for exactly this slice: one key and one bill cover object storage next to the other backend services the same worker calls, which removes a credential rotation chore rather than adding one.

One upload, one signed link: the Python code that does it

Here is the part that actually runs. Upload the original, then mint a download link when the finance UI asks for it.

import os
import time
import requests

AUTH = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}


def with_retry(send):
    """One retry policy for every call: back off on 429, honour Retry-After."""
    resp = send()
    for attempt in range(4):
        if resp.status_code != 429:
            return resp
        time.sleep(float(resp.headers.get("Retry-After", 2 ** attempt)))
        resp = send()
    return resp


def archive_receipt(tenant_id: str, receipt_id: str, pdf_bytes: bytes) -> tuple[str, str]:
    bucket = f"receipts-{tenant_id}"                 # the isolation boundary, one per tenant
    key = f"2026/{receipt_id}/original.pdf"
    resp = with_retry(lambda: requests.put(
        f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}",
        headers={**AUTH,
                 "Content-Type": "application/pdf",
                 "Idempotency-Key": f"receipt-{tenant_id}-{receipt_id}"},
        data=pdf_bytes,
        timeout=30,
    ))
    if resp.status_code >= 400:
        raise RuntimeError(f"upload rejected: {resp.status_code} {resp.text}")
    return bucket, key


def download_link(bucket: str, key: str, seconds: int = 900) -> tuple[str, str]:
    resp = with_retry(lambda: requests.post(
        f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
        headers=AUTH,
        json={"op": "get", "expires_seconds": seconds},
        timeout=30,
    ))
    if resp.status_code >= 400:
        raise RuntimeError(f"presign rejected: {resp.status_code} {resp.text}")
    signed = resp.json()
    # Hand signed["url"] straight to the browser. Never attach your platform key to it.
    return signed["url"], signed["expires_at"]

Three details in there are load-bearing. The idempotency key means a retried worker never writes the same receipt twice, which matters because a duplicated original is an audit finding, not a rounding error. The presign response carries its own expires_at, so your UI can show the user how long the link is good for instead of guessing. And the returned URL is already authenticated by its signature — sending the platform key along with it is the classic mistake, and it leaks a credential into browser history for no benefit.

There is no SDK to install for any of that. Infrai's storage calls are plain HTTP against one REST API, so the same thirty lines run from a notebook cell while I'm tuning an extraction prompt and from the container that does the work for real.

Should temporary signed links replace a permanent file download service for private exports?

For private files, yes, and the reasoning is mostly about blast radius. A permanent URL is a bearer token that never expires: forward it once in a support thread and it stays live forever. A 15-minute link forwarded to the wrong person is usually already dead. Since a receipt archive is exactly the kind of data you do not want indexed or shared sideways, the expiry is doing real security work.

The catch is that expiring links break bookmarks and emails. Send a customer a signed URL in a monthly statement email and it will be stale by the time they read it. The fix is a redirect endpoint in your own app: the emailed link points at /receipts//download, that route checks the session's tenant claim, mints a fresh signed URL, and 302s to it. Your app keeps the authorization decision, storage keeps the bytes, and neither one grows a copy of the other's job.

Prefix-only listing shapes this too. If your app database is the only place that knows which tenant owns which key, then every download path must go through code that reads that database — which is exactly the property an auditor wants to see anyway.

        timeout=30,
    ))

    ))

title: Fixed vs random effects in Python, and what a Hausman test result actually tells you
summary:
Most panel data tutorials stop at "run the Hausman test, and if p < 0.05 use fixed effects." That rule is fine as a starting point, but it hides a few things that matter once you look at real output. So here is a small worked example you can run yourself, with the numbers I got.

The setup

I used the wage_panel dataset that ships with linearmodels: 545 individuals observed over 8 years, with log wages as the outcome. The regressors are experience squared, marital status and union membership.

bash
pip install linearmodels
python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from linearmodels.panel import PanelOLS, RandomEffects
from linearmodels.datasets import wage_panel

df = wage_panel.load().set_index(["nr", "year"])
y = df["lwage"]
X = df[["expersq", "married", "union"]]

the RE model needs an intercept, the FE (within) model does not

X_re = X.copy()
X_re.insert(0, "const", 1.0)

fe = PanelOLS(y, X, entity_effects=True).fit()
re = RandomEffects(y, X_re).fit()
The two sets of estimates
variable fixed effects random effects
expersq 0.0037 0.0032
married 0.1073 0.1316
union 0.0828 0.1035

The random effects numbers for married and union are noticeably larger. That gap is what the Hausman test formalises. If the unobserved person-level effects (ability, motivation, whatever drives wages and also correlates with marrying or joining a union) are correlated with the regressors, the RE estimator picks that correlation up as if it were an effect of the regressor, and the coefficients drift upward.

Computing the Hausman statistic by hand

linearmodels doesn't ship a one-line Hausman test, but the statistic is short:

python
cols = fe.params.index
b = fe.params - re.params[cols]
V = fe.cov - re.cov.loc[cols, cols]

stat = float(b @ np.linalg.inv(V) @ b)
p = 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(stat, len(cols))
print(f"Hausman chi2 = {stat:.3f}, df = {len(cols)}, p = {p:.4f}")

Output on this data:

Hausman chi2 = 112.118, df = 3, p = 0.0000

A clear rejection. The RE assumption (effects uncorrelated with the regressors) doesn't hold here, so the fixed effects estimates are the ones to report.

Three things the textbook rule skips

A rejection is evidence against RE, not a proof that FE is right. FE only removes confounding that is constant over the sample window. Anything that changes over time and correlates with both wages and marriage is still in your error term.

You pay for FE with the time-invariant variables. The within estimator can't estimate the effect of anything that doesn't change for a person (education at entry, say, or a fixed demographic). I left those out above for exactly that reason. If they are the point of your study, FE alone won't answer your question, and a Mundlak or correlated random effects specification is worth a look.

The classic Hausman test assumes homoskedastic errors. With clustered standard errors, which is the usual choice in applied work, the difference of covariance matrices isn't the right object anymore. A regression-based version (the Mundlak approach: add the group means of each regressor to the RE model and test them jointly) works with robust errors.

If you'd rather not write code

For a quick check, or to hand something to a colleague who doesn't use Python, there is a panel data regression online tool that fits fixed and random effects models in the browser. Full disclosure: I'm connected to that site. For anything you plan to publish, I'd still keep the script above so the analysis is reproducible.
